Name: simplified_prob_iou
Title: Simplified Probabilistic Intersection over Union for Efficient Object Detection
Experiment: 1. Implement a new function `sp_iou(obb1, obb2, eps=1e-7)` that calculates a simplified probabilistic IoU. This function will use only variances (a, b) from the `_get_covariance_matrix` function, ignoring the covariance term (c). 2. Implement a hybrid function `hybrid_iou(obb1, obb2, threshold, eps=1e-7)` that uses the simplified approach when the rotation angle is below a threshold and the full `probiou` calculation otherwise. 3. Implement a function `adaptive_hybrid_iou(obb1, obb2, validation_set, eps=1e-7)` that learns the optimal threshold from a validation set. 4. Modify the `__main__` section to include tests that compare the output of `sp_iou`, `hybrid_iou`, `adaptive_hybrid_iou`, `probiou`, and `ciou` for various `obb1` and `obb2` configurations, specifically varying the rotation angle in `obb2`. 5. Measure the execution time of `sp_iou`, `hybrid_iou`, `adaptive_hybrid_iou`, `probiou`, and `ciou` for a large number of bounding box pairs. 6. Analyze the trade-off between accuracy (compared to `probiou`) and efficiency, including an analysis of the error introduced by ignoring rotation as a function of the rotation angle and the impact of the threshold in `hybrid_iou` and `adaptive_hybrid_iou`. 7. Calculate the correlation between `sp_iou`, `hybrid_iou`, `adaptive_hybrid_iou`, and `probiou` to assess their agreement in ranking bounding box pairs. 8. Train a simple object detection model with each of the IoU metrics as the loss function and evaluate their performance on a test set. 9. Discuss the application-specific considerations for choosing the appropriate IoU metric.

Name: adaptive_dynamic_prob_iou
Title: Adaptive Dynamic Complexity Probabilistic Intersection over Union with Learned Covariance Significance
Experiment: 1. Implement a new function `adaptive_dynamic_prob_iou(obb1, obb2, model, error_threshold=0.01, eps=1e-7)` that calculates ProbIOU with adaptive complexity. 2. Develop a method to train a model to predict the significance of the covariance term. The input features will include the variances (`a1`, `b1`, `a2`, `b2`), aspect ratios (`w1/h1`, `w2/h2`), and the absolute difference in rotation angles (`abs(r1-r2)`) of the bounding boxes. Two target variables will be considered: (a) the absolute difference between `probiou(obb1, obb2)` and `sp_iou(obb1, obb2)`, and (b) the relative difference: (absolute difference) / `probiou(obb1, obb2)`. A simple linear regression or a small neural network (e.g., 2 hidden layers with 10 neurons each) will be used as the model. 3. If the predicted error (either absolute or relative, based on model selection) is below `error_threshold`, the calculation will be simplified (similar to `sp_iou`), otherwise it will use the full `probiou` calculation. 4. Modify the `__main__` section to include tests that compare the output of `adaptive_dynamic_prob_iou`, `probiou`, and `sp_iou` for various `obb1` and `obb2` configurations. 5. Measure the execution time of `adaptive_dynamic_prob_iou`, `probiou`, and `sp_iou` for a large number of bounding box pairs. 6. Analyze the trade-off between accuracy (compared to `probiou`) and efficiency, including an analysis of the error introduced by simplifying the calculation as a function of the predicted covariance significance. 7. Calculate the correlation between `adaptive_dynamic_prob_iou`, `probiou`, and `sp_iou` to assess their agreement in ranking bounding box pairs. 8. Evaluate the performance of different model architectures and training strategies for predicting covariance significance, including the impact of the `error_threshold` on the accuracy-efficiency trade-off. 9. Compare the performance of models trained with absolute error versus relative error as the target variable. 10. Consider automatically determining the `error_threshold` based on application-specific requirements.

Name: adaptive_principal_axis_iou
Title: Adaptive Principal Axis-Based Approximation of Probabilistic Intersection over Union for Oriented Bounding Boxes with Learned Switching Threshold
Experiment: 1. Implement a new function `principal_axis_obb(obb)` that transforms `xywhr` format to a simplified eigen-representation using only the principal axis and the magnitudes of the projections onto the principal axis and its orthogonal axis, effectively approximating the OBB as an ellipse. 2. Implement a new function `principal_axis_iou(p_obb1, p_obb2, eps=1e-7)` that calculates IoU based on this simplified representation by approximating the intersection area of two ellipses. 3. Implement a hybrid function `adaptive_principal_axis_iou(obb1, obb2, validation_set, eps=1e-7)` that learns the optimal `ratio_threshold` from a validation set and uses `principal_axis_iou` when the eigenvalue ratio of `obb1` and `obb2` is above this threshold and `probiou` otherwise. 4. Modify the `__main__` section to include tests that compare the output of `adaptive_principal_axis_iou`, `principal_axis_iou`, `probiou`, and `sp_iou` for various `obb1` and `obb2` configurations. 5. Measure the execution time of `adaptive_principal_axis_iou`, `principal_axis_iou`, `probiou`, and `sp_iou` for a large number of bounding box pairs. 6. Analyze the trade-off between accuracy (compared to `probiou`) and efficiency, including the impact of the learned `ratio_threshold` on performance. 7. Calculate the correlation between `adaptive_principal_axis_iou`, `principal_axis_iou`, `probiou`, and `sp_iou` to assess their agreement in ranking bounding box pairs. 8. Investigate the error introduced by the simplification as a function of the ratio of the eigenvalues. 9. Evaluate the accuracy of the ellipse approximation by comparing the IoU calculated using this method with a more precise method for calculating the intersection area of two oriented rectangles. 10. Analyze the distribution of eigenvalue ratios in the validation set to understand the behavior of the adaptive switching mechanism.

Name: geo_approx_probiou
Title: Adaptive Geometric Approximation of Probabilistic Intersection over Union for Efficient Object Detection
Experiment: 1. Profile `probiou` to identify computational bottlenecks. 2. Generate diverse `obb1` and `obb2` configurations, including benchmark configurations representing various scenarios. 3. Investigate geometric models (simplified ellipse intersection, feature-based regression, hybrid approaches) for `probiou` approximation. 4. Implement `geo_approx_probiou(obb1, obb2, model_type='ellipse', params=None, eps=1e-7)` with options for different models and adaptability mechanisms (online, offline, hybrid). 5. In `__main__`, compare models using benchmark configurations, measuring approximation error (MAE, MSE, max error) and ranking performance (Kendall's tau, Spearman's correlation). 6. Measure execution times for various configurations. 7. Analyze accuracy-efficiency trade-off, including model parameter impact and visualization of error vs. geometric parameters. 8. Evaluate correlation in ranking bounding box pairs. 9. Discuss practical implications, including integration into object detection pipelines, potential performance gains, and extension to other IoU variants (CIoU, DIoU).

Name: nn_probiou
Title: Neural Network-Based Approximation of Probabilistic Intersection over Union with Enhanced Data Generation, Feature Engineering, Architecture Search, and Benchmarking
Experiment: 1. Generate a large dataset of `obb1` and `obb2` pairs with diverse configurations, covering a wide range of values for x, y, w, h, and r. Analyze the distribution of generated data. 2. Calculate the corresponding `probiou` values for each pair. 3. Experiment with feature engineering by creating new features from the raw OBB parameters, such as aspect ratios (w/h), area (w*h), relative angle difference (|r1-r2|), and potentially features derived from the covariance matrix components (a, b, c). 4. Design a fully connected neural network with an input layer that can accommodate the engineered features, a few hidden layers with ReLU activation, and an output layer with a single neuron. 5. Train the network on the generated dataset, including the engineered features, to predict `probiou`. Use MSE loss and consider L2 regularization or dropout to prevent overfitting. Tune hyperparameters like learning rate, batch size, and regularization strength. 6. Experiment with different network architectures, varying the number of hidden layers (1-3) and neurons per layer (5-50). 7. Train a linear regression model on the same dataset (with and without engineered features) as a baseline. 8. Evaluate the trained networks' and linear regression model's performance on a held-out test set, measuring MAE, MSE, and comparing them to the true `probiou` values. 9. Measure the execution time of the models' predictions for a large number of OBB pairs and compare it to the execution time of `probiou`. 10. Analyze the trade-off between accuracy and efficiency, considering the impact of model complexity and feature engineering on performance. 11. Calculate the correlation between the models' predictions and the true `probiou` values. 12. Investigate generalization using a separate test set with OBB configurations significantly different from the training data. 13. Perform error analysis to identify specific OBB configurations where the models perform poorly.

Name: geo_aware_adaptive_probiou_final
Title: Geometrically-Aware Adaptive Probabilistic Intersection over Union with Learned Interpolation and Data-Driven Alpha Selection
Experiment: 1. Implement a function `compute_geometric_features(obb1, obb2)` that computes geometric features such as aspect ratio difference, angle difference, area ratio, and a measure of shape similarity. 2. Implement a function `adaptive_probiou(obb1, obb2, decision_tree, eps=1e-7)` that uses a trained decision tree to select an interpolation parameter `alpha` (from a data-driven set) based on the output of `compute_geometric_features`. The final result will be `alpha * probiou(obb1, obb2, eps) + (1 - alpha) * sp_iou(obb1, obb2, eps)`. 3. Design a dataset generation process that creates a diverse set of OBB pairs and calculates the error between `probiou` and `sp_iou`. Determine the `alpha` values based on the quantiles of the error distribution (e.g., 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1 quantiles). 4. Train a decision tree on the generated dataset to predict the `alpha` category based on the geometric features. 5. Modify the `__main__` section to include tests that compare the output of `adaptive_probiou`, `probiou`, and `sp_iou` for various `obb1` and `obb2` configurations. 6. Measure the execution time of `adaptive_probiou`, `probiou`, and `sp_iou` for a large number of bounding box pairs. 7. Analyze the trade-off between accuracy (compared to `probiou`) and efficiency, including an analysis of how well the decision tree predicts the appropriate `alpha` category, the distribution of predicted `alpha` values, and the memory footprint of the decision tree. 8. Calculate the correlation between `adaptive_probiou`, `probiou`, and `sp_iou` to assess their agreement in ranking bounding box pairs. 9. Investigate the importance of different geometric features in the decision tree's predictions. 10. Visualize the decision boundaries of the decision tree to gain insights into the relationship between geometry and the chosen `alpha`. 11. Investigate the sensitivity of the model to decision tree hyperparameters.

Name: data_driven_hybrid_approx_probiou
Title: Data-Driven Hybrid Approximations for Efficient Probabilistic Intersection over Union
Experiment: 1. Implement a function `hybrid_approx_probiou(obb1, obb2, method_selector, error_threshold, params, eps=1e-7)` that utilizes different approximation methods for `exp()` and `log()` in `probiou`, as in the previous iteration. 2. Implement support for Taylor series (adaptive order), Pade approximants, and potentially other methods. 3. Generate a dataset of inputs and corresponding outputs for `exp()` and `log()` within the relevant range for `probiou`. For each input, determine the most accurate approximation method among the available options for a given `error_threshold`. 4. Train a model (e.g., decision tree, small neural network) to predict the best approximation method based on the input to `exp()` or `log()`. The `method_selector` argument will be this trained model. 5. Modify the `__main__` section to compare `hybrid_approx_probiou` (with different trained `method_selector` models, and a heuristic-based selector as a baseline), `probiou`, and a version using `torch.exp()` and `torch.log()` directly. 6. Measure execution times for various configurations. 7. Analyze the accuracy-efficiency trade-off, including the performance of different `method_selector` models and the impact of the data-driven selection strategy. 8. Calculate correlation to assess agreement in ranking bounding box pairs. 9. Investigate the sensitivity of the output to the accuracy of the `exp()` and `log()` approximations, and the accuracy of the `method_selector` model. 10. Consider using a lookup table for coefficients of different approximation methods for optimization.

Name: math_adaptive_simplified_probiou_final
Title: Adaptive Mathematical Simplification of Probabilistic Intersection over Union with Optimized Region Partitioning and Evaluation
Experiment: 1. Implement a function `analyze_probiou_terms(obb1, obb2, eps=1e-7)` that calculates `probiou` and returns the individual values of `t1`, `t2`, `t3`, `bd`, and `hd`. 2. Generate a diverse set of `obb1` and `obb2` configurations. 3. For each configuration, use `analyze_probiou_terms` to collect term values. 4. Analyze the distribution of each term's values. 5. Implement a function `perturb_term(obb1, obb2, term_name, perturbation_factor, eps=1e-7)` that modifies a specific term by the `perturbation_factor` before calculating `probiou`. 6. Based on the term distribution analysis, select a set of perturbation factors. 7. For each configuration and each term, measure the change in `probiou` output when the term is perturbed. 8. Analyze the sensitivity of `probiou` to each term. 9. Implement different region partitioning methods in a function `define_simplification_regions(obb1, obb2, method='method_name')`, including: (a) decision tree-based, (b) grid-based (using quantiles of geometric features), and (c) model-based (e.g., Gaussian Mixture Model). 10. For each region partitioning method, visualize the defined regions and analyze their homogeneity in terms of term sensitivity and distribution within each region. 11. For each region and partitioning method, define a specific simplification strategy based on the sensitivity and distribution analysis. 12. Implement the adaptive simplified formula in a function `adaptive_simplified_probiou(obb1, obb2, method='method_name', eps=1e-7)` that determines the region of the OBB pair and applies the corresponding simplification strategy based on the chosen partitioning method. 13. Compare the output of `adaptive_simplified_probiou` (with different partitioning methods), `simplified_probiou` (non-adaptive), and `probiou` for various configurations, measuring MAE, MSE, and execution time. 14. Calculate the Pearson correlation and a rank-based correlation measure (e.g., Kendall's tau) between `adaptive_simplified_probiou`, `simplified_probiou`, and `probiou`. 15. Evaluate and compare the performance of different region partitioning methods to determine the most effective approach in terms of accuracy, efficiency, and region homogeneity.

Name: term_selective_probiou
Title: Term-Selective Optimization of Probabilistic Intersection over Union with Learned Term Significance and Adaptive Computation
Experiment: 1. Implement a function `calculate_term_contributions(obb1, obb2, eps=1e-7)` that calculates `probiou` and returns `t1`, `t2`, `t3`, along with their relative contributions to `bd` (e.g., `t1/bd`, `t2/bd`, `t3/bd`). 2. Generate a diverse set of `obb1` and `obb2` configurations. 3. For each configuration, use `calculate_term_contributions` to collect term values and contributions. Analyze distributions and correlations with geometric features (e.g., aspect ratio, angle difference, area ratio), including visualizations. 4. Train a model (e.g., decision tree, random forest, or a small neural network) to predict the significance of each term based on geometric features. 5. Implement `term_selective_probiou(obb1, obb2, significance_model, thresholds={t1: 0.05, t2: 0.1, t3: 0.2}, eps=1e-7)` that uses the model to predict term significance. If a term's predicted significance is below its `threshold`, approximate it: a) If below a lower threshold (e.g., 50% of the main threshold), set the term to 0. b) Otherwise, use a pre-trained linear regression model (trained separately for each term) based on the term's value range observed in the training data. If above the threshold, use the full calculation. 6. Modify `__main__` for tests comparing `term_selective_probiou`, `probiou`, and `sp_iou`, and measure execution times for a large number of bounding box pairs. 7. Analyze the trade-off between accuracy and efficiency, including the accuracy of term significance predictions (using precision, recall, F1-score), the impact of `thresholds`, and simplification effectiveness. 8. Calculate correlations between `term_selective_probiou`, `probiou`, and `sp_iou`. 9. Investigate the model's sensitivity to geometric features and architecture. 10. Determine optimal `thresholds` data-drivenly using a validation set, exploring different optimization strategies (e.g., grid search, Bayesian optimization) to find the best threshold combination that balances accuracy and efficiency. 11. (Optional) Analyze the joint distribution of term contributions to explore potential interactions between terms and investigate whether a more holistic simplification approach could be beneficial.

Name: contribution_adaptive_probiou_optimized
Title: Optimized Contribution-Adaptive Probabilistic Intersection over Union with Jointly Learned Thresholds
Experiment: 1. Implement a function `analyze_term_contributions(obb1, obb2, eps=1e-7)` that calculates `probiou` and returns `t1`, `t2`, `t3`, `bd`, `hd`, and the relative contributions of `t1`, `t2`, and `t3` to `bd`. 2. Generate a diverse set of `obb1` and `obb2` configurations. 3. For each configuration, use `analyze_term_contributions` to collect term values and contributions. 4. Analyze distributions and correlations with geometric features. 5. Train a model to predict term contributions based on geometric features. This model will also predict the `contribution_thresholds` for each term. 6. Implement `contribution_adaptive_probiou(obb1, obb2, trained_model, eps=1e-7)` that uses the `trained_model` to predict both term contributions and their corresponding thresholds. If a contribution is below its predicted threshold, either set the term to 0 or use a constant approximation based on training data statistics. Otherwise, use the full calculation. 7. Define a composite loss function that combines: (a) the error in predicting term contributions, (b) the error introduced by the simplification (difference between `probiou` and the output of `contribution_adaptive_probiou`), and (c) a regularization term that encourages larger thresholds (e.g., L1 or L2 regularization on the thresholds). 8. Train the model using this composite loss, jointly learning to predict contributions and optimize thresholds. 9. Modify `__main__` for tests comparing `contribution_adaptive_probiou`, `probiou`, and `sp_iou`. 10. Measure execution times. 11. Analyze the trade-off between accuracy and efficiency, including the accuracy of contribution predictions, the learned thresholds and their impact on simplification, and the effectiveness of the simplified approximations. 12. Calculate correlations between `contribution_adaptive_probiou`, `probiou`, and `sp_iou`.

Name: symmetry_monotonicity_optimized_probiou_final
Title: Exploiting Symmetry and Targeted Monotonicity for Efficient Probabilistic Intersection over Union with Data-Driven Simplifications
Experiment: 1. Implement a function `test_symmetry(obb1, obb2, eps=1e-7, tolerance=1e-5)` that calculates `probiou(obb1, obb2)` and `probiou(obb2, obb1)` and returns the absolute difference. 2. Generate a diverse set of `obb1` and `obb2` configurations. 3. Use `test_symmetry` to empirically test for symmetry across the generated configurations. 4. Analyze the distribution of the differences and determine if they are consistently below the `tolerance`, indicating symmetry. 5. If symmetry is confirmed, implement a function `symmetry_probiou(obb1, obb2, eps=1e-7)` that only calculates `probiou` for one ordering of inputs and reuses the result. This function will only be used if the empirical test confirms symmetry. 6. Implement a function `explore_monotonicity(obb1, obb2, param, values, eps=1e-7)` that calculates `probiou` while varying a specific parameter (`param`) of `obb2` across a range of `values` while keeping other parameters constant. Focus on `param` being the angle difference and the distance between centers. 7. Analyze the output of `explore_monotonicity` to identify potential monotonic relationships with respect to the angle difference and distance between centers, using visualizations like line plots. 8. Based on the findings, design and implement a function `monotonicity_optimized_probiou(obb1, obb2, eps=1e-7)` that incorporates checks for specific conditions identified as having monotonic relationships. If these conditions are met, use a simplified calculation or bounding strategy based on the observed monotonic behavior. 9. Analyze the ordering of bounding boxes in a typical object detection pipeline (e.g., by examining the output of a standard NMS algorithm) to assess the potential impact of the symmetry optimization. 10. Modify the `__main__` section to include tests comparing the output and execution time of `symmetry_probiou` (if implemented), `monotonicity_optimized_probiou` (if implemented), and `probiou`. 11. Measure execution times and analyze the accuracy of the optimized functions. Evaluate `monotonicity_optimized_probiou` by also analyzing the frequency with which simplification conditions are met and the magnitude of error introduced by simplifications. 12. Calculate correlations.

Name: error_aware_learned_hybrid_ellipse_probiou
Title: Error-Aware Learned Hybrid Ellipse-Based Approximation for Efficient Probabilistic Intersection over Union
Experiment: 1. Implement a function `obb_to_ellipse(obb)` that transforms an OBB from `xywhr` format to an ellipse representation `(cx, cy, a, b, theta)`, where `(cx, cy)` is the center, `a` and `b` are the semi-major and semi-minor axis lengths, and `theta` is the orientation angle. 2. Implement a function `ellipse_iou(ellipse1, ellipse2, eps=1e-7)` that calculates an approximate IoU of two ellipses based on their parameters. 3. Generate a diverse dataset of `obb1` and `obb2` pairs and calculate their ellipse representations using `obb_to_ellipse`. 4. For each pair, calculate both `ellipse_iou` and `probiou`. 5.
